name: Date
tagline: The most useful complication of all: today's date, in a small window.
summary: A rotating disc printed with 1 to 31 shows the day of the month through an aperture in the dial. It is by far the most common complication in the world.
howItWorks: A 24-hour wheel in the motion works carries a finger that engages the teeth of a 31-tooth date ring once a day. Around midnight the finger pushes the ring forward by one tooth, and a spring-loaded jumper snaps it neatly into place so the numeral sits squarely in the window. Instantaneous dates store energy in a spring for a few hours and release it at midnight for a crisp jump. Because the ring always has 31 positions, a simple date must be advanced by hand at the end of any shorter month, usually by pulling the crown to its first position.
history: Pointer dates appeared on pocket watches in the 18th century, but the modern date window arrived on the wrist in the 1930s and 1940s. Rolex's Datejust of 1945 popularised the self-winding date that changes automatically at midnight, and its Cyclops magnifier followed in 1953. Today the date is standard on most mechanical and quartz watches.
funFact: Setting a simple date between about 9 pm and 3 am can damage some movements, because the date wheels are already engaged.

name: Chronograph
tagline: A stopwatch on the wrist, started, stopped and reset with pushers.
summary: A chronograph adds a stopwatch to a watch. The central seconds hand starts and stops on demand, and small subdials count the elapsed minutes and hours.
howItWorks: The chronograph is a second mechanism that borrows power from the running watch. Pressing the start pusher engages a clutch, either a lateral coupling of toothed wheels or a vertical friction clutch, linking the seconds train to the chronograph seconds wheel. A column wheel or a cheaper cam lever system coordinates start, stop and reset. A second press disengages the clutch and a brake holds the hand still. The reset pusher drops hammers onto heart-shaped cams, whose shape always returns the hands to zero from any position.
history: Louis Moinet built a timer running at 60 beats a second in 1816 to follow astronomical observations, and Nicolas Rieussec patented a recording chronograph in 1821. Adolphe Nicole's heart-shaped reset cam of 1844 made the modern chronograph possible. Wrist chronographs followed around 1913, and 1969 brought the first automatic versions from Zenith, Heuer-Breitling and Seiko.
funFact: The Omega Speedmaster was the only watch to pass NASA's 1965 qualification tests and went to the Moon in 1969.

name: GMT (second time zone hand)
tagline: An extra 24-hour hand keeps a second time zone in view.
summary: A GMT watch adds a fourth hand that turns once a day against a 24-hour scale, showing the time in a second place. With a rotating bezel it can track a third.
howItWorks: An extra wheel geared from the hour wheel turns at half its speed, carrying the GMT hand once around the dial every 24 hours. Read against a 24-hour scale on the dial or bezel, it shows home time while the main hands show local time, and the 24-hour scale also tells you whether it is day or night at home. In a 'true' or flyer GMT the local hour hand can be jumped in one-hour steps without stopping the watch, which is handy after landing; in a 'caller' or office GMT, it is the GMT hand that jumps instead.
history: Rolex developed the GMT-Master with Pan Am in 1954 so that crews on transatlantic flights could read Greenwich Mean Time, then the reference for aviation. Its red and blue 'Pepsi' bezel split day and night. Rolex's GMT-Master II of 1982 added the independently adjustable hour hand, and the complication has since become a staple of sports watches.
funFact: The original GMT-Master's bezel was made of Bakelite and was prone to cracking, so Rolex switched to aluminium.

name: Moon phase
tagline: A painted moon waxes and wanes across the dial, month after month.
summary: A moon phase display shows where the moon is in its 29.5-day cycle, usually as a golden moon disc passing behind two humps in an aperture.
howItWorks: A disc painted with two moons on a starry background sits beneath a shaped aperture. The disc has 59 teeth and is advanced one tooth each day by a finger on the calendar works, so each moon takes two days per tooth pair, or 29.5 days per cycle. Because the real synodic month is 29 days, 12 hours and 44 minutes, this common version gains one day every two and a half years and needs a manual nudge. The two humps of the aperture, called bosses, hide the moon disc to mimic its waxing and waning shape.
history: Astronomical clocks showed the moon's phases from the Middle Ages, and pocket watches carried them from the 16th century. The display became a favourite of 20th-century calendar watches, especially alongside a triple calendar or perpetual calendar, and survived the quartz era as an emblem of traditional watchmaking.
funFact: Fishermen and farmers once relied on moon phases to plan tides and planting, which is why rural pocket watches often carried them.

name: Power reserve indicator
tagline: A fuel gauge for the mainspring: how long before the watch stops.
summary: A power reserve indicator shows how much energy is left in the mainspring, usually as a hand sweeping across a small arc from full to empty.
howItWorks: The indicator needs to know the difference between how much the mainspring has been wound and how much it has run down. A differential gear, like the one in a car axle, takes one input from the winding side of the barrel and one from the running side, and its output turns the indicator hand. When you wind, the hand rises; as the watch runs, it falls. A simpler design uses a threaded arbor on which a small nut travels up and down with the barrel's rotation.
history: Abraham-Louis Breguet and others fitted up-and-down indicators to marine chronometers and pocket watches in the late 18th century, where knowing when to wind was vital for navigation. The display migrated to wristwatches in the 1940s and 1950s and remains popular on manually wound and long-reserve movements.
funFact: German makers label the gauge 'Auf' and 'Ab', meaning up and down.

name: Perpetual calendar
tagline: Knows every month's length and every leap year, correct until 2100.
summary: A perpetual calendar shows date, day, month and leap year, and automatically accounts for months of 28, 29, 30 and 31 days. It needs no correction until 1 March 2100.
howItWorks: At the heart of the mechanism is a program wheel that turns once every four years. Its edge is cut with notches of different depths for each month, with a shallower notch for February and a deeper one for leap-year Februaries. At the end of each month a feeler lever drops into the notch, and its depth decides how far the date is advanced, skipping days 29, 30 or 31 as needed. A great lever carries the information around the dial, driving the day, month, moon and leap-year displays in a single cascade at midnight.
history: The English watchmaker Thomas Mudge built a perpetual calendar pocket watch around 1762. Patek Philippe made the first perpetual calendar wristwatch in 1925, using a movement originally intended for a pendant watch. Audemars Piguet's thin automatic perpetual of 1978 and IWC's crown-adjustable Da Vinci of 1985 brought the complication back after the quartz crisis.
funFact: The year 2100 is not a leap year under the Gregorian calendar, so almost every perpetual calendar will need a correction then.

name: Tourbillon
tagline: The escapement set spinning in a cage to average out gravity.
summary: A tourbillon mounts the balance wheel and escapement in a rotating cage, usually turning once a minute, to cancel out positional errors caused by gravity.
howItWorks: In a normal watch, gravity pulls slightly on the balance wheel and makes the watch run fast or slow depending on its position. The tourbillon places the whole escapement, including the balance, hairspring, pallet fork and escape wheel, in a lightweight cage that rotates, typically once a minute. The escape wheel's pinion rolls around a fixed fourth wheel, so the escapement keeps working while the cage turns. By rotating through every vertical orientation, the errors largely cancel out. The cage must be extremely light, often weighing less than a third of a gram, to avoid sapping power.
history: Abraham-Louis Breguet patented the tourbillon in Paris in 1801 for pocket watches, which spent their lives upright in a waistcoat pocket. It remained a rare prestige showpiece until modern CNC machining made it feasible in series in the 1980s and 1990s. Today it is admired more for its mesmerising motion and craftsmanship than for precision gains on the wrist.
partsCount: About 50 to 80 parts in the cage
funFact: Breguet's patent was granted on 26 June 1801, the 7th Messidor of Year IX in the French Revolutionary calendar.

name: Minute repeater
tagline: Chimes the hours, quarters and minutes on tiny gongs, on demand.
summary: At the slide of a lever, a minute repeater strikes the time: low tones for the hours, double tones for the quarters and high tones for the minutes since.
howItWorks: Pulling the slide on the case winds a separate spring and releases the striking train. Stepped cams called snails, one each for hours, quarters and minutes, are read by feeler racks whose depth sets how many blows each hammer strikes. Two hammers hit wire gongs curled around the movement, tuned by hand to harmonise. A centrifugal or inertial governor keeps the cadence steady so the chime is neither rushed nor dragged. An all-or-nothing piece ensures the watch strikes the full time or nothing at all.
history: Repeating watches were invented in England in the 1680s, credited to Daniel Quare and Edward Barlow, so the time could be told in the dark before electric light. Breguet introduced wire gongs around 1783, making repeaters thinner and more resonant. Today only a few hundred are made each year, and each is tuned by a specialist watchmaker.
funFact: Patek Philippe's CEO personally listens to every minute repeater before it leaves the manufacture.
